newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Market uncertainty delays Ivory coffee campaign.
newsitem.headline: Market uncertainty delays Ivory coffee campaign.

text.p: Ivory Coast has postponed an announcement on the opening of its 1996/97 coffee marketing campaign because of world price fluctuations, industry sources say.
Ivorian Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan told an industry review on Wednesday that the date would most likely be set for late 1996 or early 1997.
The Ivory Coast has in recent years announced the date and price for its coffee marketing campaign in September, at the same time that it sets the date and price for its cocoa marketing campaign.
"They have probably postponed for a technical reason. They don't know what price to set," one analyst said.
"But there's plenty of coffee out there and some traitants might be offering low prices. Some farmers will have to sell before a price is set."
Farmers need money in early October to pay school fees.
Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze told Wednesday's review producer country losses had not been stemmed even though world stocks were at their lowest in seven years.
World prices have fallen since the Ivory Coast set the 1995/96 producer price of 700 CFA per kilo of bagged coffee and trade sources expect a cut in the rate when it is set for 1996/97.

Robusta coffee futures slid to more than two-year lows of $1,471 a tonne on September 20 1996 after touching near 10-year highs of $4,140 a tonne in September 1994, following frosts and drought in Brazil, the world's largest producer.
Slides in robusta futures reflect higher retail prices, which have bitten into world consumption, and a recovery in global production led by Brazil, analysts say.
Gauze said the future of the cocoa sector in Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, was looking good.

"It could be the same for coffee. Let's not prejudge the outcome of the next meeting in London of coffee producing countries which will decide measures and other management instruments for regulating next year's coffee campaign," he added.

Traders and Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) delegates in London said they were not expecting any fireworks at the ACPC meeting on Friday and Saturday as the group's mandate is to contemplate the effectiveness of last year's and this year's export plans.

Analysts in Abidjan say the government is making heavy losses. "For every tonne sold there is a margin of loss for the government. Under the bareme (the price scale covering the whole marketing chain), total costs are higher than the world price," one said.
Effective government price support in September was about 100 CFA franc a kilo but had been as high as 200 CFA, he added.
"The IMF and the World Bank will not accept this and the farm prices will go down to perhaps to 400 or 500 CFA a kilo," he added.
An IMF "illustrative calculation" suggests the farm-gate price could be pared to 480 CFA a kilo.

Traders and exporters expect a cut of anywhere between 50 and 250 CFA a kilo but expect little change in cocoa prices as next year's crop is already forecast down and disincentives to production appear unnecessary.

Ivory Coast aims to produce 350,000 tonnes of coffee a year by 2002. Forecasters put the 1995/96 total at 170,000 tonnes against 194,000 in 1994/95 but the 1996/97 crop is expected to exceed 200,000 due to good farm maintenance.
Cumulative exports in the first 11 months of the 1995/96 (Oct-Sept) season were 137,150 tonnes against 108,184 tonnes in the same period of 1994/95.
Some traders and exporters said they expected a coffee price to be set in mid-November.
Ivory Coast opened this year's 1995/96 coffee marketing season on October 7 with an official recommended producer price of 700 CFA a kilo for bagged coffee.

The minimum farm-gate indicator price included a five CFA payment towards the coffee sack and exporters had largely paid that price, Gauze said. The recommended price in 1994/95 was 650 CFA loose, but some exporters paid over 800 CFA a kilo.
A June government statememt said 324,486 hectares of coffee were rehabilitated in 1994/95 against a targeted 300,000 hectares.
